title: General Principles of Metallurgy: Extraction of Elements
subcategory: General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements — Ore Concentration, Reduction, Refining

references.label: NCERT Chemistry Part I, Class 12 — General Principles and Processes of Isolation of Elements

summary: Extracting a metal from its ore follows a general sequence — concentration, conversion to oxide, reduction, and refining — with the SPECIFIC reduction method chosen based on the metal's reactivity, guided quantitatively by the Ellingham diagram (a plot of Gibbs energy of oxide formation vs. temperature).
explanation: The general metallurgical sequence is: (1) CONCENTRATION of the ore (removing unwanted gangue/impurities, by methods like froth flotation for sulphide ores, or magnetic separation, chosen based on the physical/chemical differences between ore and gangue); (2) CONVERSION to oxide — ROASTING (heating a sulphide ore in excess air, converting it to an oxide and releasing SO₂) or CALCINATION (heating a carbonate/hydroxide ore in LIMITED air/absence of air, releasing CO₂/water vapour) — a frequently tested distinction based on the type of ore and the atmosphere used; (3) REDUCTION of the oxide to the free metal; (4) REFINING to remove remaining impurities from the crude metal. The choice of REDUCTION method depends strongly on the metal's reactivity/position in the reactivity series: highly reactive metals (Na, K, Ca, Mg, Al) require ELECTROLYTIC reduction (of a molten salt/oxide, since they are too reactive to be reduced by ordinary chemical reducing agents); moderately reactive metals (Fe, Zn, Pb, Cu) are typically reduced using a chemical reducing agent (like carbon/coke, or via self-reduction for some ores); and less reactive/noble metals (Ag, Au, Hg) often occur naturally in free (uncombined) form or are easily reduced by simple heating alone. The ELLINGHAM DIAGRAM plots the standard Gibbs energy of formation (ΔG°) of various metal oxides against temperature; a metal whose oxide-formation line lies LOWER (more negative ΔG°) at a given temperature can reduce the oxide of any metal whose line lies ABOVE it at that same temperature — this is precisely why carbon (whose line has a notably steep, DOWNWARD-shifting slope, unlike most metals, due to the entropy increase in forming gaseous CO/CO₂) becomes a progressively more effective reducing agent at higher temperature, and is used industrially (e.g. in the blast furnace) to reduce iron oxide at high temperature, even though it wouldn't work as well at lower temperature. REFINING methods include electrolytic refining (impure metal as anode, pure metal deposits at cathode — used for copper, for example) and zone refining (exploits different solubility of impurities in molten vs. solid metal, used for extremely high-purity semiconductor-grade materials like silicon and germanium).
commonMisconceptions: Confusing roasting (sulphide ores, EXCESS air, produces oxide + SO₂) with calcination (carbonate/hydroxide ores, LIMITED/absent air, produces oxide + CO₂ or H₂O) — mixing up which process applies to which type of ore, or which atmosphere is used, is a very frequent exam error.

Assuming carbon can reduce ANY metal oxide at any temperature simply because it's a common, cheap reducing agent — the Ellingham diagram shows carbon only becomes thermodynamically favourable as a reducing agent for certain oxides ABOVE a specific crossover temperature; below that, other reducing agents may work better.

Believing highly reactive metals like sodium or aluminium could be extracted using ordinary carbon reduction — their oxides are far too thermodynamically stable (very negative ΔG°) for carbon to reduce under practically achievable conditions, which is exactly why electrolytic reduction is essential for them instead.
examples: Iron oxide is reduced by carbon monoxide (generated from coke) in a blast furnace at high temperature, exploiting the favourable crossover point on the Ellingham diagram.
Aluminium is extracted from purified alumina by electrolytic reduction (the Hall-Héroult process), since it is far too reactive to be reduced by carbon under practical conditions.
genZNote: Ellingham diagram: carbon's reducing power gets better with heat, unlike basically every metal's.
